notes:
I found commentary on every verse. Three gaps:
- **Not found:** anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this psalm (v. 16 or v. 19 would be the likely verses); anything from oca.org or bibleodyssey.org; and any Pentecostal or Wesleyan writer who differs from the others on a particular verse.
- **Partial:** the Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 16. For vv. 17–21 I only have short search excerpts from it.
- **Labels:** several Bible Hub and StudyLight pages show excerpts without naming the commentator. Where that happened I say "an unnamed commentator" rather than guess.

The clearest disagreement between Protestant traditions is at v. 9. The Catholic and Orthodox material I found comes from the newadvent.org page and the Douay-Rheims and Greek (Septuagint) translations.

---

**Introduction / title**
- "A psalm of praise" (Hebrew *tehillah*) appears as a title only here in the Psalms. This is the first of the last six psalms, which are full of praise. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-15.html
- A writer Spurgeon quotes suggests the name was kept for the last of David's psalms to show that everything he wrote ends in praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- Jewish practice was to recite this psalm three times a day. (VanGemeren, quoted by Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- **Acrostic:** each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, but the letter *nun* is missing. See v. 13. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21993
- **Modern scholarship:** Perowne says the heading "of David" can't be trusted for this psalm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-15.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: David praises God directly ("You"), personally ("my God"), with a surrendered heart ("O King"), and without end. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- Spurgeon: David, God's king, worships God as his own King. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- Pulpit Commentary: better read "my God, the King," the only King of heaven and earth. It adds that "forever" implies the writer believed in his own immortality. https://biblehub.com/psalms/145-1.htm
- An unnamed commentator: the speaker may be Israel as a people. If it is one person, he forgets his own death while praising the eternal King. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/145-1.htm
- **Reading "King" as Christ:** Gill takes "the King" as the King Messiah. https://studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/145-1.html Thomas Le Blanc, quoted by Spurgeon, calls Christ our God and King. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** "Praise of David" means praise of Christ, who came from David's line. He also urges readers to start praising now if they mean to praise forever. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801145.htm

**v. 2**
- Spurgeon: praise every day, whatever kind of day it is. Love for God isn't kept for holy days. Moving from "bless Your name" to "bless You" brings David closer to God himself. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- Spurgeon also notes the four "I will"s: praise can't be done by someone else on your behalf. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- NET Bible note: "forever" may be poetic exaggeration. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon: a great God deserves great praise. In God, greatness means splendid goodness. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- A writer Spurgeon quotes: God is not praised at all unless he is praised greatly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- JFB: Psalm 48:1 borrows this line. The verse begins the list of what God's "name" (v. 2) includes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-145.html
- NET Bible: "no one can fathom his greatness." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 4**
- Guzik: older people can stir up younger ones by remembering God's past acts, and younger people can stir up older ones by telling what God is doing now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- Spurgeon: each generation adds a chapter, and together they make one great book. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- **NET Bible (grammar):** the verbs could state what the psalmist expects ("will praise") or what he wishes ("may they praise"). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 5**
- A writer Spurgeon quotes says "muse" or meditate is a better translation than "speak." These truths should be thought over deeply until they shape our character. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-145.html
- Guzik: praise comes from careful thought as well as feeling. David thought about who God is as well as what he has done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/

**v. 6**
- JFB: the Hebrew has two readings here, singular "greatness" and plural "great deeds." The plural matches "awesome acts" better. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-145.html
- Guzik: the psalm keeps returning to two reasons for praise, who God is and what he has done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon: God's righteousness frightens sinners, but believers sing about it. Because Jesus died in their place, righteousness now guarantees the salvation of the redeemed. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- A writer Spurgeon quotes says only the cross shows righteousness in forgiving sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- Guzik, citing Spurgeon: the Hebrew word for "extol" (KJV "utter") suggests bubbling up or overflowing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/

**v. 8**
- This verse repeats Exodus 34:6, a great hope for sinners. Calvin called it as clear a description of God's nature as can be found anywhere. (Cole) https://bible.org/book/export/html/21993
- Constable defines the terms: grace is undeserved favour, mercy is holding back deserved wrath, and loyal love is strong and lasting. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-9.html
- An unnamed commentator: God's real will leans toward favour. Wrath is only the background, released reluctantly after long waiting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/145-9.htm

**v. 9 — the main disagreement between traditions**
- **Shared reading:** Guzik calls this "common grace," God's goodness to everyone, like sun and rain on the evil and the good (Matthew 5:45). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- **Reformed (Calvin):** God is good to everyone without distinction. Because sin brought the whole world under a curse, his mercy reaches even the animals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-9.html
- **Baptist, strongly Calvinist (Gill):** "all his works" in the second line means the new creatures in Christ (Ephesians 2:10), who share God's special mercy. It doesn't mean all created things. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-9.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** God's mercy rests on every soul outside hell. He did not decree anyone's damnation before they were created, and Jesus died for every person. Clarke calls the decree of reprobation (God choosing some for damnation) "Molochian." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-9.html
- **Matthew Henry:** God is good to all his creatures except devils and the damned, who shut themselves out. His mercy shows most clearly in the "vessels of mercy." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-9.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** draw on 1 Timothy 4:10 to separate God's general care for all from saving grace. https://biblehub.com/psalms/145-9.htm
- **Anglican Prayer Book wording:** an unnamed commentator says the meaning is wider than the Prayer Book Version's "unto every man." It means all creation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/145-9.htm
- Spurgeon says this verse supports a duty to be kind to animals. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- Horne (quoted by Guzik) and another writer Spurgeon quotes: the word for "tender mercies" comes from the Hebrew for "womb," like a mother's love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- **Catholic and Greek texts:** the Douay-Rheims reads "The Lord is sweet to all." Brenton's translation of the Greek reads "good to those that wait on him." https://biblehub.com/psalms/145-9.htm

**v. 10**
- A writer Spurgeon quotes: people have more reason to praise God than other creatures, and believers more than other people, because they have received grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- Another writer in Spurgeon's notes: creation shows God's skill without knowing it. When believers praise out of love and gratitude, praise becomes "blessing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/145.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** warns against thinking that stones or animals understand God, while saying that God has ordered every level of creation. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801145.htm

**v. 11**
- Spurgeon's sermon on this verse: "they" are the saints of v. 10. Their talk about God's kingdom and power should mark them out as believers. He applies the "kingdom" to Christ's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-145.html
- Maclaren (quoted by Guzik): those who receive God's grace should be its messengers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/

**v. 12**
- Spurgeon: people quickly forget God's acts, so his people must keep teaching them to every generation. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php

**v. 13**
- Spurgeon: the psalmist switches from "his" to "your" as he comes near to God. God's reign has no beginning, break or end. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps145.php
- Meyer: these words are carved on a Damascus mosque that used to be a church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/psalms-145.html

**The missing *nun* line** (the second half of BSB v. 13: "faithful in all His words…")
- The traditional Hebrew text has no *nun* line. One medieval Hebrew manuscript, the Qumran scroll from Cave 11, the Greek Septuagint and the Syriac all include it. NET says scholars are divided. L. C. Allen argues it is original, but NET asks why it would have been dropped by accident and suggests a later editor added it. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145
- **Ellicott:** the line probably dropped out, but the version found in the ancient translations looks suspicious. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-13.html
- **Clarke:** the line was lost because it looks so much like v. 17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-145.html
- **Gill:** reports a Talmud tradition that David left it out because he foresaw Israel's fall in Amos 5:2, a prophecy that begins with *nun*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-13.html
- **McGee:** it was left out deliberately, because praise is incomplete until Christ's kingdom comes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-13.html
- **Cole:** it may well be original, but we can't be certain. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21993

**v. 14**
- A writer Spurgeon quotes: God shows his kingdom's might by helping the weak, not by crushing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- Spurgeon's sermon: a paradox. Those who fall into Christ's arms are the only ones who stand. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-145.html
- Guzik and Kidner: God gives timely help to those who are falling and revives lost hope. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- NET: "bowed down" may mean discouraged. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 15**
- Calvin: God acts like the father of a household feeding everyone. He notes that some interpreters limit this to humans because of the word "hope." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-15.html
- Matthew Henry: animals "wait on" God by the instinct he gave them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/145-15.html
- Guzik: people pray "give us this day our daily bread." Clarke pictures young animals looking to their parents for food. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- **Lutheran use:** vv. 15–16 form the table prayer in Luther's Small Catechism. An LCMS writer says she prefers it to the common "Come, Lord Jesus" prayer because of its strong biblical core. https://witness.lcms.org/2021/come-lord-jesus/

**v. 16**
- JFB: literally "satisfy every living thing with what it desires," compare v. 19. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-145.html
- Utley at bible.org: vv. 14–16 deal with physical needs and vv. 17–21 with spiritual needs. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-145
- Bible Hub: Jesus feeding the crowds acts out God "opening his hand." https://biblehub.com/psalms/145.htm

**v. 17**
- A writer Spurgeon quotes (in the style of Calvin): people praise God's justice but complain when trouble comes. The verse defends God's righteousness "in all his ways." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: God answering prayer shows the grace described earlier in the psalm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- Matthew Henry: God is always within call of his people's prayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/145.htm
- Meyer: the Lord is near even when we don't sense it. Saying this verse often is a way of practising God's presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/psalms-145.html
- NET: "in truth" means sincerely. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 19**
- JFB: God fulfils desires when that is good for us and fits his will. He answers just as truly when he withholds harmful things. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-145.html
- Spurgeon's notes give examples of desires God rightly refuses because they are sinful or not for our good, such as David's wish to take revenge on Nabal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- Trapp (quoted by Guzik): Luther could pray "Let my will be done" only because his will was for God's will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- **Reformed note:** a writer Spurgeon quotes says that desires turned toward God are evidence of God's electing love. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps145.cfm
- **NET:** in context, "desire" means the desire to be rescued from wicked enemies. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: those destroyed have made themselves fit for destruction. Destroying the wicked is also how God protects his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/145.htm

**v. 21**
- Matthew Henry: some people will bless God forever, and he wishes all would. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/145.htm
- Guzik quotes a writer who says this is David's last recorded word in the Bible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-145/
- NET: "every creature" is literally "all flesh." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=145
- Bible Hub links it to every creature praising God in Revelation 5:13. https://biblehub.com/psalms/145.htm
